lesson.title: Chemical Messengers: How Neurons Talk Across the Gap
lesson.summary: Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers released by a neuron's axon terminal in response to an arriving action potential, and they cross the synaptic gap to bind receptors on the next cell, translating an electrical signal back into a chemical one.
lesson.body:
An action potential can carry a signal electrically down an axon at remarkable speed, following the all-or-none pattern established earlier, but neurons almost never touch each other directly. A tiny gap called the synaptic cleft separates the presynaptic axon terminal from the postsynaptic dendrite or cell body of the next neuron. Neurotransmitters exist to solve exactly this problem: they are how an electrical signal gets converted into a chemical one that can physically cross that gap and potentially start a brand new electrical signal on the other side.

The process begins with neurotransmitter molecules already synthesized and packaged inside small membrane-bound sacs called synaptic vesicles, stored near the axon terminal. When an arriving action potential reaches the terminal, it opens voltage-gated calcium channels, letting Ca2+ flow into the cell. That calcium influx triggers the vesicles to fuse with the terminal's membrane and release their neurotransmitter contents into the synaptic cleft, a process called exocytosis.

Once released, neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the narrow cleft and bind to specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane, fitting them the way a key fits a lock. That binding opens ion channels, producing either an excitatory effect, such as Na+ flowing in and depolarizing the membrane toward threshold as described in the discussion of synaptic threshold, or an inhibitory effect, such as chloride flowing in or potassium flowing out and hyperpolarizing the membrane away from threshold. Whether a given neurotransmitter is excitatory or inhibitory at a given synapse depends on which receptor and which channel it activates there, not on some fixed property of the molecule itself.

For the system to reset and respond to the next signal, the neurotransmitter's action in the cleft has to be shut off quickly, and this happens in one of two main ways. Reuptake involves transporter proteins on the presynaptic terminal pulling the released neurotransmitter back inside for reuse. Enzymatic degradation instead breaks the neurotransmitter down chemically within the cleft, as acetylcholinesterase does to acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Certain nerve agents and insecticides work by blocking that exact enzyme, leaving acetylcholine active far too long and causing uncontrolled, continuous muscle stimulation.

This entire chemical relay is happening at every synapse described back in the reflex arc, including the connections linking sensory neurons to interneurons and interneurons to motor neurons in the spinal cord. Dozens of distinct neurotransmitters exist in the nervous system, each with its own typical receptors, pathways, and effects on behavior. Four in particular come up constantly in psychology, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, and glutamate, and each is examined individually next.
